34 A cell has an electromotive force (e.m.f.) of 6 V and internal resistance R. An external resistor,
also of resistance R, is connected across this cell, as shown.
cell
6 V
R
R
Power P is dissipated by the external resistor.
The cell is replaced by a different cell that has an e.m.f. of 6 V and negligible internal resistance.
What is the new power that is dissipated in the external resistor?
A
0.5P
B
P
C
2P
D
4P

hints: Notice the first circuit has the internal resistance $R$ in series with the external resistor $R$, so the total resistance is $2R$ for e.m.f. $6\text{ V}$.
Recall power in the external resistor is $P=I^2R$, so first find the current $I=E/R_{total}$ in each case.
Compare the second circuit where internal resistance is negligible, so total resistance is only $R$ and the full $6\text{ V}$ is across the external $R$.
walkthrough: First circuit: internal $R$ and external $R$ are in series, so $R_{total}=R+R=2R$.
Current is $I_1=E/R_{total}=6/(2R)=3/R$ with units $\text{A}$ if $R$ is in $\Omega$.
Power in external $R$ is $P=I_1^2 R=(3/R)^2 R=9/R$.
Second circuit: negligible internal resistance, so $R_{total}=R$ and current is $I_2=6/R$, which is twice $I_1$.
Ratio $P_{new}/P=(36/R)/(9/R)=4$, so $P_{new}=4P$. This is option D.

A.explanation: This would mean power halves, but removing internal resistance increases current and terminal p.d., so power must increase.

B.explanation: Power cannot stay the same because the total resistance falls from $2R$ to $R$ while e.m.f. stays at $6\text{ V}$.

C.explanation: This assumes power is proportional to current, but for fixed $R$ power is $I^2R$, so doubling current quadruples power.

D.explanation: Current doubles from $3/R$ to $6/R$ and $P=I^2R$ increases by $2^2=4$, giving $4P$.
